pathways.climate_pressure: Rainfall deficits and associated livelihood stress.
pathways.documented_impact: The 2012–2019 departmental study finds higher subsequent US family-unit apprehensions associated with rainfall shortfalls.
pathways.fcv_mediator: Higher homicide rates strengthen the observed relationship; the authors interpret unsafe internal alternatives as a possible mobility constraint.
pathways.possible_consequence: Cross-border movement may reflect intertwined livelihood and safety concerns; the study does not establish that drought causes violence or individual migration.
alternative_explanations: Wealth, networks, enforcement/apprehension patterns, poverty, governance and household preferences influence migration.
pathways.uncertainty: Observational aggregate models using department of birth, not necessarily pre-departure residence; author interpretation is not a directly tested household mediation chain.
resilience_factors: The authors propose farmer participation and agricultural resilience alongside governance/security measures; effects are not evaluated.
pathways.compact_statement: Honduras evidence finds a stronger rainfall-deficit/migration association in higher-violence departments; the proposed safety constraint is interpretive, not causal proof.

gaps: Observed associations concern departmental birthplace and apprehension records, not all migration or a causal effect. Water-allocation disputes are not attributed to drought from co-location.

executive_assessment.text: Selected Pespire, San Lorenzo and El Corpus communities add household coping, land access and definition-specific mobility evidence.
The Duke models report weather–violence interaction in migration associations; local water/coastal concerns are separately reported and must not be spliced into a causal violence chain.
Goascorán cooperation and WFP commitments provide capacity context, not independently verified peace gains.
